description.checks: Fast Image calls that must work as the app's first, before any view has loaded an image.

cache-path-web-at-start.checks: FastImage.getCachePath for a cache: 'web' image works as the app's first Fast Image call (Android failed, saying Glide isn't set up: the HTTP cache of web images was only set up once a view had loaded an image).
cache-path-web-at-start.steps: With no image view on screen, calls FastImage.getCachePath with cache: 'web' for a photo the image server marks as cacheable for an hour (a new url each run), which downloads it into the HTTP cache. Passes when the result is ok.
cache-path-web-at-start.shows: An empty gray square: the case shows no image.

description.checks: #436: a FastImage's open sides follow the loaded image, as an 's do: the other side from its aspect ratio, or its own size with neither set.

auto-size-width.checks: An image with only a width (in a row) gets the height its aspect ratio gives.
auto-size-width.steps: Loads a 600x300 photo with style { width: 240 } in a row. Passes once it has loaded and its layout is 240x120.
auto-size-width.shows: The photo at 240x120 on the left, not stretched.

auto-size-height.checks: An image with only a height (in a row) gets the width its aspect ratio gives.
auto-size-height.steps: Loads the 600x300 photo with style { height: 64 } in a row. Passes once it has loaded and its layout is 128x64.
auto-size-height.shows: The photo at 128x64 on the left.

auto-size-natural.checks: An image with no size (in a row) is its own size: a 120x120 image is 120x120 points.
auto-size-natural.steps: Loads a 120x120 photo with no style in a row. Passes once it has loaded and its layout is 120x120.
auto-size-natural.shows: The 120x120 photo at 120x120 points on the left.

auto-size-auto.checks: A height of 'auto' is open, as no height is.
auto-size-auto.steps: Loads the 600x300 photo with style { width: 240, height: 'auto' } in a row. Passes once it has loaded and its layout is 240x120.
auto-size-auto.shows: The photo at 240x120 on the left.

auto-size-scale.checks: A bundled @3x image with no size is its size in points: its pixels over its file's scale.
auto-size-scale.steps: Shows require('./images/center-dot.png'), only a 120x120 @3x file, with no style in a row. Passes once it has loaded and its layout is 40x40.
auto-size-scale.shows: A 40x40 blue square on the left.

description.checks: #436, continued: an SVG's own size, a FastImageBackground's image, and how an image with only a width is decoded and shown as it loads.

auto-size-svg.checks: An SVG with no size is its own size: a 24x24 SVG is 24x24 points.
auto-size-svg.steps: Loads a 24x24 SVG of a black ring with no style in a row. Passes once it has loaded and its layout is 24x24.
auto-size-svg.shows: A 24x24 black ring on the left.

auto-size-background.checks: A FastImageBackground's image fills it: its insets (absoluteFill) set its size, which doesn't follow the image.
auto-size-background.steps: Shows the 600x300 photo in a 160x160 FastImageBackground. Passes once it has loaded and the image is 160x160.
auto-size-background.shows: The photo covering a 160x160 square (its middle).

auto-size-downsample.checks: An image with only a width is decoded for its size, as one with both sides set is: they look the same.
auto-size-downsample.steps: Loads a 1600x1000 page of text at 128x80, and again (another url) with only a width of 128, which follows the image to 128x80. Passes once both have loaded.
auto-size-downsample.shows: The same text page twice, at 128x80, with the same sharpness. A blurrier or more aliased right one means it was decoded at another size.

auto-size-cover.checks: An image with only a width and objectFit cover shows the whole image as it loads, not a crop of its middle for a size the view doesn't get.
auto-size-cover.steps: Records the left quarter of a 240x120 box, then loads a 600x300 image of magenta, cyan and magenta thirds into it with style { width: 240 }, until 1.5 s after onLoad. Passes when the recording sees magenta, and never cyan.
auto-size-cover.shows: The image at 240x120: magenta, cyan and magenta thirds.

description.checks: #436, continued: padding, and a height a later style clears.

auto-size-padding.checks: With padding, the image (which fills the view, padding included) has its aspect ratio: the padding isn't added to it.
auto-size-padding.steps: Loads the 600x300 photo with style { width: 96, padding: 8 } in a row. Passes once it has loaded and its layout is 96x48.
auto-size-padding.shows: The photo at 96x48 on the left.

auto-size-cleared.checks: A height a later style clears (height: undefined, as StyleSheet.flatten takes it) is open.
auto-size-cleared.steps: Loads the 600x300 photo with style [{ height: 200 }, { width: 96, height: undefined }] in a row. Passes once it has loaded and its layout is 96x48.
auto-size-cleared.shows: The photo at 96x48 on the left.

auto-size-padding-cover.checks: An image with only a width, padding and objectFit cover shows the whole image as it loads, not a crop of it for the padding's strip.
auto-size-padding-cover.steps: Records the point 10 points below the top of a 240x128 box, then loads a 600x300 image whose top fifth is magenta and the rest cyan into it with style { width: 240, padding: 8 }, until 1.5 s after onLoad. Passes when the recording sees magenta, and never cyan.
auto-size-padding-cover.shows: The image at 240x120: a magenta band at the top over cyan.

description.checks: #436, continued: a url placeholder, several sizes, a source change and a failed one, of an image with only a width.

auto-size-placeholder.checks: A url placeholder of an image with only a width is decoded for that width, so another view showing the same placeholder shows it whole.
auto-size-placeholder.steps: Shows a photo the slow server sends over about 35 s, with style { width: 240 } and a placeholder url of a 600x300 image of magenta, cyan and magenta thirds. 2.5 s later, a 128x64 view with another slow photo and the same placeholder mounts. Passes then.
auto-size-placeholder.shows: The thirds at 128x64: magenta, cyan and magenta. A single smeared color means the placeholder was decoded 1 pixel high.

auto-size-source-change.checks: An image with only a width and objectFit cover whose source changes to an image of another shape shows the whole new image, not a crop of it for the previous image's shape.
auto-size-source-change.steps: Loads a 120x120 photo with style { width: 240 } (240x240), then records the point 8 points below the view's top while the source changes to a 600x300 image whose top fifth is magenta and the rest cyan, until 1.5 s after its onLoad. Passes when the recording sees magenta, and never cyan.
auto-size-source-change.shows: The 600x300 image at 240x120: a magenta band at the top over cyan.

auto-size-sources.checks: With several sizes of an image and only a width, the size for that width loads, and only that one.
auto-size-sources.steps: Loads a 256x256 and a 1024x1024 size of a photo as source, with style { width: 64 } in a row. Passes when, 2 s after onLoad, the server got one request for the 256 px one and none for the 1024 px one.
auto-size-sources.shows: The photo at 64x64 on the left.

auto-size-failed.checks: An image with only a width whose source changes to one that fails is 0 high again, as before an image loaded, not the previous image's height.
auto-size-failed.steps: Loads the 600x300 photo with style { width: 96 } in a row (96x48), then changes the source to a url that 404s. Passes when, 1 s after onError, its layout is 96x0.

description.checks: onLoadEnd's event: whether the load worked, with onLoad's size or onError's error.

load-end-ok.checks: onLoadEnd's event has the load's result: for an image that loads, ok: true and the same width and height onLoad got.
load-end-ok.steps: Loads the logo from the image server, with onLoad and onLoadEnd. Passes once both have fired and onLoadEnd's event is { ok: true, width, height } with onLoad's size.
load-end-ok.shows: The React logo (light blue) on the gray square.

load-end-error.checks: onLoadEnd's event has the load's result: for an image that fails, ok: false and the same error onError got.
load-end-error.steps: Loads a url the image server answers with a 404, with onError and onLoadEnd. Passes once both have fired and onLoadEnd's event is { ok: false, error } with onError's error.
load-end-error.shows: An empty gray square: the image never loads.

description.checks: Event handlers and source values that crashed or failed loads: tintColor without an image, handlers removed after firing, source values Fast Image doesn't know, and images without handlers.

tint-remote.checks: tintColor on a remote image without a defaultSource (#1082: iOS crashed tinting an image with no size, before the remote one had loaded).
tint-remote.steps: Loads the logo with tintColor green and no defaultSource. Passes on onLoad.
tint-remote.shows: The React logo in solid green instead of its usual light blue.

tint-404.checks: tintColor on an image that fails to load (#1082: iOS crashed tinting an image with no size).
tint-404.steps: Loads a url the image server answers with a 404, with tintColor green. Passes on onError.
tint-404.shows: An empty gray square: nothing loads, so there's nothing to tint.

remove-onLoad.checks: Removing the onLoad handler after it has fired (#1088: iOS called the removed handler and crashed).
remove-onLoad.steps: Loads the logo with onLoad; when it fires, the case re-renders without onLoad. Passes once it has fired; a crash after that fails the whole run.
remove-onLoad.shows: The React logo (light blue) on the gray square.

remove-onLoadEnd.checks: Removing the onLoadEnd handler after it has fired (#1088: iOS called the removed handler and crashed).
remove-onLoadEnd.steps: Loads the logo with onLoadEnd; when it fires, the case re-renders without onLoadEnd. Passes once it has fired; a crash after that fails the whole run.
remove-onLoadEnd.shows: The React logo (light blue) on the gray square.

remove-onError.checks: Removing the onError handler after it has fired (#1088: iOS called the removed handler and crashed).
remove-onError.steps: Loads a url the image server answers with a 404 with onError; when it fires, the case re-renders without onError. Passes once it has fired; a crash after that fails the whole run.
remove-onError.shows: An empty gray square: the image never loads.

unknown-cache.checks: A source.cache that isn't one of Fast Image's values ('sometimes') is treated as the default ('immutable') instead of failing.
unknown-cache.steps: Loads the logo with cache: 'sometimes'. Passes on onLoad.
unknown-cache.shows: The React logo (light blue) on the gray square.

react-native-reload.checks: React Native Image's cache: 'reload', which Fast Image doesn't have, is treated as the default instead of failing.
react-native-reload.steps: Loads the logo with cache: 'reload'. Passes on onLoad.
react-native-reload.shows: The React logo (light blue) on the gray square.

unknown-priority.checks: A source.priority that isn't one of Fast Image's values ('urgent') is treated as the default ('normal') instead of failing.
unknown-priority.steps: Loads the logo with priority: 'urgent'. Passes on onLoad.
unknown-priority.shows: The React logo (light blue) on the gray square.

non-string-cache.checks: A source.cache that isn't a string (the number 1) is treated as the default instead of failing or crashing.
non-string-cache.steps: Loads the logo with cache: 1. Passes on onLoad.
non-string-cache.shows: The React logo (light blue) on the gray square.

no-handlers.checks: Images without event handlers send no events to JS (they sent onLoadStart, onLoad and onLoadEnd anyway, work for nothing on the JS thread).
no-handlers.steps: Loads one photo in three images: the first two have no handlers, the third has onLoadEnd. Counts every Fast Image event React Native receives from the first two. Passes if, half a second after the third's onLoadEnd, none arrived.
no-handlers.shows: Three copies of the same photo (a pug in a blanket).

data-uri-cache-only.checks: A data uri with cache: 'cacheOnly' loads: its data is the app's own, so cache doesn't apply (it's never downloaded). Android's Glide never loaded one (onlyRetrieveFromCache).
data-uri-cache-only.steps: Loads an 8×8 yellow PNG data uri with cache: 'cacheOnly'. Passes on onLoad.

data-uri-utf8.checks: A percent-encoded (utf8, not base64) SVG data uri loads. Android's Glide only read base64 data uris, so it never loaded.
data-uri-utf8.steps: Loads a magenta square SVG as a data:image/svg+xml;utf8 uri, with its # written %23. Passes on onLoad.

description.checks: Sources that fail fire onError: a data uri that isn't an image, an empty or null uri, and a 404, whose error says so.

error-invalid-data-uri.checks: A data: uri whose data isn't an image fires onError (iOS fired onLoad, with a size of 0x0).
error-invalid-data-uri.steps: Loads a data:image/png;base64 uri whose data is the text 'not an image'. Passes on onError.
error-invalid-data-uri.shows: An empty gray square: nothing loads.

error-empty-uri.checks: An empty uri fires onError (#1028: Android didn't fire it).
error-empty-uri.shows: An empty gray square: nothing loads.

error-null-uri-default.checks: A null uri fires onError and shows defaultSource (#945: Android showed nothing).
error-null-uri-default.steps: Loads { uri: null } with a defaultSource bundled in the app. Passes on onError.
error-null-uri-default.shows: The defaultSource: on iOS an aerial photo of fields; on Android a text field's underline drawable (a short black line near the bottom of the gray square). An empty gray square means defaultSource didn't show.

error-null-uri-downsample.checks: A null uri with downsample fires onError (iOS crashed).
error-null-uri-downsample.steps: Loads { uri: null } with downsample. Passes on onError; a crash fails the whole run.
error-null-uri-downsample.shows: An empty gray square: nothing loads.

error-message.checks: onError's error says what went wrong (#200: onError had no details).
error-message.steps: Loads a url the image server answers with a 404. Passes when onError's error contains '404'.
error-message.shows: An empty gray square: the image never loads.

description.checks: source.headers that isn't an object of strings (null, an array, values that aren't strings) on views and in FastImage.preload, and a uri that isn't a string.

headers-null.checks: headers: null (e.g. a header object built only when signed in) is treated as no headers, and the image loads (Android crashed).
headers-null.steps: Loads the logo with headers: null. Passes on onLoad.
headers-null.shows: The React logo (light blue) on the gray square.

headers-array.checks: headers given as an array doesn't stop the image loading (Android crashed).
headers-array.steps: Loads the logo with headers: ['x-token']. Passes on onLoad.
headers-array.shows: The React logo (light blue) on the gray square.

headers-non-string.checks: Header values that aren't strings are left out and the string ones still sent (Android crashed; iOS sent no headers at all when one wasn't a string).
headers-non-string.steps: Loads a photo from the image server's /private/ path, which answers 403 without the header x-token: fast-image, with headers { 'x-token': 'fast-image', 'x-null': null, 'x-object': {} }. Passes on onLoad, which needs x-token to have been sent.
headers-non-string.shows: A photo of a bear on rocks, filling the square. An empty gray square means the string header wasn't sent (a 403).

uri-non-string.checks: A uri that isn't a string fires onError.
uri-non-string.shows: An empty gray square: nothing loads.

headers-invalid-preload.checks: FastImage.preload with headers: null, headers as an array, or header values that aren't strings preloads each source, and sends the string headers (Android crashed).
headers-invalid-preload.steps: Preloads three sources: the logo with headers: null; the logo with headers: ['x-token']; a photo from the /private/ path (403 without x-token: fast-image) with a string x-token next to a null and an object value. Passes when every result is ok.
headers-invalid-preload.shows: An empty gray square: preload shows no image.

description.checks: Props and calls that crashed the app or never loaded: defaultSource without a source, FastImage.preload with missing or unresolvable uris, asset:/ uris (Android), and views with a width or height of 0.

default-no-source.checks: defaultSource with no source at all (#973: Android crashed).
default-no-source.steps: Renders a FastImage with only a defaultSource bundled in the app. Passes if the app is still running 750 ms after it mounts.
default-no-source.shows: The defaultSource: on iOS an aerial photo of fields; on Android a text field's underline drawable (a short black line near the bottom of the gray square).

preload-no-uri.checks: FastImage.preload with sources that have no uri, or a null source (#774: Android crashed).
preload-no-uri.steps: Calls FastImage.preload with { uri: '' }, {}, { uri: null } and null. Passes if the app is still running 750 ms later.
preload-no-uri.shows: An empty gray square: the case shows no image.

preload-unresolved.checks: FastImage.preload with a uri that can't be resolved, a bare file name (#849: Android crashed).
preload-unresolved.steps: Calls FastImage.preload with { uri: 'not-a-real-image.jpg' }. Passes if the app is still running 750 ms later.
preload-unresolved.shows: An empty gray square: the case shows no image.

asset-uri.checks: asset:/ uris are Android only (#1068), so there's nothing to check on iOS and tvOS.
asset-uri.steps: Renders an empty placeholder. Passes 750 ms after it mounts.

zero-size.checks: An image in a view with a width and height of 0 still loads and fires onLoad (#865: Android never fired it).
zero-size.steps: Loads a photo with style { width: 0, height: 0 }. Passes on onLoad.
zero-size.shows: Nothing: the view has no size.

zero-height.checks: An image in a view with a width but a height of 0 still loads and fires onLoad (#865: Android never fired it).
zero-height.steps: Loads a photo with style { width: 64, height: 0 }. Passes on onLoad.

description.checks: Layout and sizes: onLayout, measure through refs, images in the app by name, tintColor in style, and the image size onLoad reports.

layout.checks: onLayout reports the image's position in its parent (#992: it came from the inner native view, which reported 0).
layout.steps: Loads the logo with marginLeft: 10 and onLayout. Passes once the image has loaded and onLayout has reported x = 10.
layout.shows: The React logo (light blue) on a gray square, 10 dp in from the left.

ref-measure.checks: measure and measureInWindow, called through FastImage's and FastImageBackground's refs, report the size of the view the image fills (#1254 typed these refs; this checks they reach that view).
ref-measure.steps: Loads the logo in a 48×48 FastImage and a 96×48 FastImageBackground, each with a ref. Once both have loaded, calls measure and measureInWindow through each ref. Passes if they report 48x48, 48x48, 96x48 and 96x48.
ref-measure.shows: The React logo on a gray square, then the logo in a wide box, scaled up to its width and cropped at the top and bottom (cover).

app-image-name.checks: An image in the app by its name (in the asset catalog on iOS, a drawable on Android) loads (#410: iOS looked for a file of that name in the app's resources, which an asset catalog image isn't, so it didn't load).
app-image-name.steps: Loads { uri: 'regression_quadrants' }. Passes when onLoad reports 80x80, the image's size.
app-image-name.shows: The quadrants filling the square: red top left, green top right, blue bottom left, yellow bottom right.

tint-style.checks: tintColor in style tints the image, as with React Native's Image (#946: iOS ignored it).
tint-style.steps: Loads the logo with style tintColor: 'green'. Passes on onLoad.
tint-style.shows: The React logo in solid green instead of its usual light blue. A light blue logo means the tint was ignored.

source-size.checks: onLoad reports the image's own size, not the size it was decoded at for the view (#608: Android reported the size of the smaller bitmap it decoded).
source-size.steps: Loads a 600×300 photo into a 48×48 view with objectFit="contain". Passes when onLoad reports 600x300.
source-size.shows: A wide photo of green cliffs, letterboxed: gray above and below it.

source-size-gif.checks: onLoad reports a GIF's own size too, not the size it was decoded at for the view (#608).
source-size-gif.steps: Loads a 500×281 animated GIF of a jellyfish into a 48×48 view with objectFit="contain". Passes when onLoad reports 500x281.
source-size-gif.shows: The jellyfish GIF (a pink and orange jellyfish on deep blue), letterboxed: gray above and below it. Animated, so it isn't compared.

source-size-cached.checks: onLoad reports the image's own size when the image comes from a cache, too.
source-size-cached.steps: Loads the 1000×1000 logo (on Android from the app's assets, so the third load comes from Glide's disk cache of resized images, which it only uses for local images) three times: decoded, from the memory cache, and after FastImage.clearMemoryCache(). Passes if every onLoad reported 1000x1000; the image is removed after the third.
source-size-cached.shows: An empty gray square: the image is removed once its third load has been checked.

description.checks: View style props on FastImage's single native view: borders, radii, padding, overflow, opacity, transforms, shadows, backfaceVisibility and tintColor, drawn and clipped as on a View.
description.steps: Every image but the last is the same wide photo of green cliffs (2:1) with the default objectFit cover, in a 56 dp square or a 96×56 box. Each case passes once its images have loaded; the screenshot does the checking.

style-corners.checks: Per-corner and logical corner radii, with a border: the image is clipped inside the border, with the matching inner radii.
style-corners.steps: Two squares: one with corner radii 0 (top left), 24 (top right), 8 (bottom right) and 16 (bottom left) and a 3 dp blue border; one with borderTopStartRadius and borderBottomEndRadius 24.
style-corners.shows: Left: the photo inside a blue border, its top left corner square, the top right much rounder than the bottom ones, and no photo outside the border. Right: the photo with its top left and bottom right corners rounded.

style-border-sides.checks: Borders of a different width and color on each side, a 50% radius on a wide box, and a dashed border.
style-border-sides.steps: Three images: a square with borderRadius 12 and borders of 2 (red, top), 6 (green, right), 10 (blue, bottom) and 4 (orange, left); a 96×56 box with borderRadius '50%'; a square with borderRadius 8 and a 2 dp dashed black border.
style-border-sides.shows: Left to right: the photo framed by a thin red top, green right, thick blue bottom and orange left border, with rounded corners; the photo clipped to an ellipse; the photo inside a dashed black border with rounded corners.

style-padding.checks: padding doesn't inset the image, which fills the box as without padding, and overflow: 'visible' with a radius leaves the image's corners square.
style-padding.steps: Three squares: padding 8 with a 2 dp black border and borderRadius 12; the same border and radius without padding; borderRadius 16 with overflow: 'visible'.
style-padding.shows: Left to right: two identical photos inside rounded black borders, filling them (a gap inside the left border is the bug); a photo with square corners.

style-effects.checks: opacity, a rotation, a box shadow and elevation on the image, each with a radius but the first.
style-effects.steps: Four squares: opacity 0.5; borderRadius 12 rotated 15 degrees; borderRadius 12 with boxShadow '0 4px 8px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.6)'; borderRadius 12 with elevation 8.
style-effects.shows: Left to right: the photo at half opacity; rounded and tilted clockwise; rounded with a dark shadow below; rounded, with a soft shadow on Android only (elevation is Android only).

style-backface.checks: backfaceVisibility on an image turned around (rotateY 180°): 'hidden' doesn't show it, and 'visible' shows it mirrored.
style-backface.steps: Two squares with transform rotateY: '180deg': backfaceVisibility 'hidden', then 'visible'.
style-backface.shows: Left: nothing at all, not even the gray background. Right: the photo mirrored, the cliffs on the left.

tint-prop-wins.checks: The tintColor prop wins over tintColor in style, as with React Native's Image.
tint-prop-wins.steps: Loads the logo with objectFit="contain", tintColor green and style tintColor red.
tint-prop-wins.shows: The React logo in solid green on a gray square. A red logo means style's tintColor won.

description.checks: Style changes after the image has loaded (a border removed, overflow switched) and a gradient background, each next to an image that should look the same.
description.steps: Each case passes a moment after its change (the gradient on onLoad); the screenshot does the checking.

style-gradient.checks: A gradient background (experimental_backgroundImage) shows under a contained image, as on a View (Android drew no gradient on FastImage's view).
style-gradient.steps: Loads the wide photo with objectFit="contain" in a square with experimental_backgroundImage linear-gradient(#ff0000, #0000ff), next to a View with the same gradient. Passes on onLoad.
style-gradient.shows: Left: the photo across the middle, with the gradient's red above it and blue below. Right: the whole gradient, red at the top to blue at the bottom.

style-border-change.checks: A border removed after the image has loaded: the image fills the box again (Android kept the image it had loaded for the smaller box inside the border, stretched).
style-border-change.steps: Loads a 600×300 photo in two 96×56 boxes; the left one has a 40 dp black top border, removed 100 ms after onLoad. Passes 1 s later.
style-border-change.shows: Two identical photos of green cliffs filling their boxes. A black band at the top of the left one, or the photo stretched, is the bug.

style-border-removed.checks: One edge's border width removed after the image has loaded, under a width for every edge: that edge falls back to the width for every edge, and the image stays inside the borders (on Android with React Native 0.83 to 0.87, the removed width reached the view as NaN and the image was drawn over the left border).
style-border-removed.steps: Loads a 600×300 photo in two 96×56 boxes with a 6 dp black border; the left one also has borderLeftWidth 30, removed 100 ms after onLoad. Passes 1 s later.
style-border-removed.shows: Two identical photos inside even 6 dp black borders. A thick left border, or the photo over the left border, is the bug.

style-overflow-change.checks: overflow switched from 'hidden' to 'visible' after the image has loaded, with a borderRadius: the corners become square, as on an image that was visible from the start (iOS kept the rounded mask).
style-overflow-change.steps: Loads the wide photo in two squares with borderRadius 16; the left one starts with overflow: 'hidden', switched to 'visible' 100 ms after onLoad. Passes 1 s later.
style-overflow-change.shows: Two identical photos of green cliffs with square corners. Rounded corners on the left one are the bug.

description.checks: Changes after load, checked by screenshot (tintColor removed, objectFit changed, a view that gets taller), and a GIF without a loop count, checked by a video sample.

clear-tint.checks: tintColor removed after the image has loaded shows it untinted again (#586: iOS kept the tint).
clear-tint.steps: Loads the logo twice: the right one with tintColor green, removed in its onLoad. Passes 500 ms later.
clear-tint.shows: Two identical light blue React logos. A green right one is the bug.

fit-change.checks: objectFit changed from cover to contain after the image has loaded (#762: Android kept showing the cover crop).
fit-change.steps: Loads a 600×300 photo in two squares: the left with objectFit="contain", the right with cover, switched to contain in its onLoad (the same source object throughout: a new one reloaded the image, which hid the bug). Passes 750 ms later.
fit-change.shows: Two identical photos of green cliffs, letterboxed: gray above and below. A right one that fills its square is the bug.

gif-loop-once.checks: A GIF without a loop count plays once and stops on its last frame (#651: Android looped every GIF forever).
gif-loop-once.steps: A video sample: the screen is recorded while the case shows a GIF of two 0.4 s frames, magenta then cyan, with no loop count and no loop prop, until 2.4 s after onLoad; the color in the middle of the view must go from gray to magenta to cyan, and stay cyan.
gif-loop-once.shows: A cyan square: the last frame. In the recording: gray, magenta, cyan; magenta again after cyan means it looped.

size-change.checks: An image in a view that gets taller after it has loaded looks like React Native's Image next to it (#983: Android showed a zoomed-in slice, since Glide had cropped the image for the first size).
size-change.steps: Loads a 600×1200 image of 12 px black and white vertical stripes with objectFit cover in a 96×16 view, next to React Native's Image with resizeMode cover; 300 ms after onLoad, both views become 96×96. Passes 1 s later.
size-change.shows: Two identical squares of thin black and white vertical stripes. Wider stripes on the left (zoomed in) are the bug.

description.checks: The loop and paused props on GIFs: stopping after one or two plays, looping a GIF that plays once, changing loop, pausing, and resuming.
description.steps: The GIFs have two frames of a solid color each (0.4 s each, unless a case says otherwise); each case waits for its plays after onLoad.

gif-loop-false.checks: loop={false} plays a GIF that loops forever by itself once, and it stops on its last frame.
gif-loop-false.steps: Loads a GIF that loops forever, red then blue, with loop={false}. Passes 1.4 s after onLoad (one play and a margin).
gif-loop-false.shows: A blue square: the last frame. Red means it was still playing.

gif-loop-count.checks: loop={2} plays a GIF that loops forever by itself twice, and it stops on its last frame.
gif-loop-count.steps: Loads a GIF that loops forever, orange then purple, with loop={2}. Passes 2.2 s after onLoad (two plays and a margin).
gif-loop-count.shows: A purple square: the last frame. Orange means it was still playing.

gif-loop-true.checks: loop (true) keeps a GIF that plays once by itself looping.
gif-loop-true.steps: Loads a GIF without a loop count, yellow then green, with loop. Passes 1.4 s after onLoad if the app hasn't crashed.
gif-loop-true.shows: A yellow or green square: it's animated, so it's not compared.

gif-loop-change.checks: loop changed from false to true after the GIF has stopped plays it again, and it keeps looping.
gif-loop-change.steps: Loads a GIF that loops forever by itself, orange then purple, with loop={false}; 1.4 s after onLoad (it has stopped on purple), sets loop to true. Passes 0.4 s later if the app hasn't crashed.
gif-loop-change.shows: An orange or purple square: it's animated, so it's not compared.

gif-paused.checks: paused: a GIF that loops forever by itself stays on its first frame.
gif-paused.steps: Loads the image (red, then blue, 400 ms each, looping) with paused. Passes a play's length (0.8 s) after onLoad.
gif-paused.shows: A red square (the first frame); blue would mean it played.

gif-resume.checks: paused, then paused={false}, with loop={false}: the image plays once and stops on its last frame.
gif-resume.steps: Loads an image that loops forever by itself (red, then blue, 400 ms each) with paused and loop={false}. A play's length (0.8 s) after onLoad, it sets paused={false}. Passes a play (and a margin) later.
gif-resume.shows: A blue square (the last frame); red would mean resuming didn't play it.

gif-resume-finished.checks: A GIF that has finished its one play, paused and then resumed, plays again from the start, on both platforms (as iOS's player does).
gif-resume-finished.steps: Loads a GIF that plays once: 1.5 s red, then 0.1 s blue. 2.2 s after onLoad (its play is over) sets paused, and 0.2 s later unpauses it. Passes 0.3 s later, while it shows its first frame again.
gif-resume-finished.shows: A red square (a slightly darker red than the paused case's): the first frame, playing again. Blue means it didn't play again.

description.checks: imageRendering auto, smooth (iOS only) and pixelated, on images drawn smaller and larger than their size.

image-rendering-stripes.checks: imageRendering on an image drawn much smaller than its size: smooth (iOS only; the same as auto on Android) averages its pixels.
image-rendering-stripes.steps: Shows 1024 px black and white stripes, 1 px each, at their own size (a 200×24 strip of them), then drawn at 48 points with imageRendering auto, smooth and pixelated, from the full image (downsample={false}). Passes when the three have loaded; the screenshot does the checking.
image-rendering-stripes.shows: A strip of fine stripes, then three squares, left to right auto, smooth and pixelated. On iOS smooth is an even gray (#445), and auto and pixelated show uneven stripes; on Android all three show wide, even bands (moiré): soft gray in auto and smooth, sharp black and white in pixelated.

image-rendering-text.checks: imageRendering on a page of small text drawn much smaller than its size: smooth (iOS only; the same as auto on Android) keeps the lines of text continuous.
image-rendering-text.steps: Draws a 1600×1000 page of small text at 96×64 points with imageRendering auto, smooth and pixelated, from the full image (downsample={false}). Passes when the three have loaded; the screenshot does the checking.
image-rendering-text.shows: The page three times, left to right auto, smooth and pixelated. On iOS smooth has continuous gray lines of text, and auto and pixelated broken ones; on Android all three are broken up.

image-rendering-pixel-art.checks: imageRendering on an image drawn larger than its size: pixelated keeps its pixels sharp (#926).
image-rendering-pixel-art.steps: Shows 12 px pixel art at its own size, then drawn at 64 points with imageRendering auto, smooth and pixelated. Passes when the three have loaded; the screenshot does the checking.
image-rendering-pixel-art.shows: A tiny sprite, then three large ones, left to right auto, smooth and pixelated: auto and smooth blurred, pixelated with sharp square pixels.

image-rendering-change.checks: imageRendering changed after load, from pixelated to auto: on iOS the image moves onto whole pixels then, as sharp as auto from the start.
image-rendering-change.steps: Loads a 1600x1000 page of text into two 40x96 views with downsample and cover: the left with imageRendering="pixelated", changed to auto once both have loaded, the right with auto. Passes once it has changed; the screenshot does the checking.
image-rendering-change.shows: Two tall crops of the middle of the page, the same and both sharp. A blurry left one is a failure.

description.checks: blurRadius: how much it blurs (in points, whatever the file's size), on other kinds of image, changed after load, and not on defaultSource.

blur.checks: blurRadius is in points: blurRadius={6} looks about the same as React Native's Image on iOS, and the same from a large file and a small one, since the image is blurred at the size it's shown at. The blurred views don't change an unblurred one of the same file.
blur.steps: Four 64 dp squares: FastImage with a 1024 px photo, no blur; React Native's Image with the same photo and blurRadius={6}; FastImage with the same photo and blurRadius={6}; FastImage with a 256 px file of the photo and blurRadius={6}. Passes 0.5 s after all four have loaded.
blur.shows: A sharp photo of green cliffs, then three blurred alike. On Android the second (React Native's Image) is nearly sharp: it blurs in the file's pixels, and this file is large.

blur-kinds.checks: blurRadius on other kinds of image: a bundled image, a tinted one, and a GIF, which shows its first frame, blurred and still.
blur-kinds.steps: Shows a bundled photo with blurRadius={6}; the logo with tintColor green, blurRadius={4} and objectFit="contain"; a jellyfish GIF with blurRadius={6}. Passes 0.5 s after all three have loaded.
blur-kinds.shows: A blurred aerial photo of fields; a soft green React logo on gray; the jellyfish's first frame, blurred and not moving (a pink and orange blur on blue).

blur-change.checks: blurRadius changed once the image has loaded blurs or unblurs the image that's showing, without load events (Android loaded the image again, with its events).
blur-change.steps: Four photos of a pug: the first loads with blurRadius 0, set to 6 after its onLoadEnd; the second has 6 from the start; the third loads with 6, set to 0 after its onLoadEnd; the fourth has no blur. Fails if onLoadStart, onProgress, onLoad or onLoadEnd fires on the first or third after that; passes 1.5 s after both changes.
blur-change.shows: Two pugs blurred alike, a gap, then two sharp ones alike.

blur-default-source.checks: blurRadius doesn't blur defaultSource, as with React Native's Image.
blur-default-source.steps: Loads a url the image server answers with a 404, with a bundled defaultSource and blurRadius={6}. Passes on onError.
blur-default-source.shows: The defaultSource, sharp: on iOS an aerial photo of fields, on Android a gray square with a short black line near the bottom.

description.checks: tintColor changed on a blurred image after it has loaded.

blur-tint-change.checks: tintColor changed on a blurred image after it has loaded shows the new color, blurred, like an image tinted that color from the start (iOS shows it without blurring the image again).
blur-tint-change.steps: Loads the logo twice with blurRadius={4} and objectFit="contain": the left with tintColor green, changed to purple (#9324c3) 300 ms after both have loaded; the right purple from the start. Passes 500 ms after the change.
blur-tint-change.shows: Two identical blurred purple React logos on gray. A green or sharp left one is the bug.

description.checks: blurRadius changed in quick steps after the image has loaded: no load events fire again, and the image ends up with the last radius.

blur-change-twice.checks: blurRadius changed twice, 300 ms apart, after a slow cache: 'web' image has loaded: no load events fire again, and it ends up like an image blurred that much from the start (Android loads the image again for each new blur; a change during that load started the image's load again, which sent onProgress, onLoad and onLoadEnd).
blur-change-twice.steps: Loads a photo of a pug with cache: 'web' and onProgress from the slow server, which sends no cache headers, so each load downloads it again (in about 2 s). After its onLoadEnd, sets blurRadius 5, then 10 300 ms later. Fails if a load event fires after that first onLoadEnd or onProgress didn't fire before it; passes 4 s after the last change.
blur-change-twice.shows: Two photos of a pug blurred alike: the one that changed, and one with blurRadius 10 from the start.

blur-change-steps.checks: blurRadius changed in five steps in renders right after each other (before the next frame), as an animated blur or a slider changes it, after the image has loaded: no load events fire again, and it ends up like an image blurred that much from the start.
blur-change-steps.steps: Loads a photo of a pug. After its onLoadEnd, renders blurRadius 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10, each its own commit. Fails if a load event fires after that first onLoadEnd; passes 4 s after the last step.
blur-change-steps.shows: Two photos of a pug blurred alike: the one that changed, and one with blurRadius 10 from the start.

description.checks: objectFit's values, checked by screenshot: images larger and smaller than the view, an SVG, with blurRadius, in style, and changed after load.

object-fit.checks: objectFit's five values place a larger image in its view as CSS's object-fit does.
object-fit.steps: Loads the 600x300 image into five 48-point views with objectFit fill, contain, cover, none and scale-down. Passes once all five have loaded (and a moment more); the screenshot checks the fits.
object-fit.shows: Five 48-point views of the 600x300 image (red with a blue border): fill stretched to the square, the border all around; contain whole, half the height, with gray above and below; cover showing the middle, the border only at the top and bottom; none showing the middle at its own size, red only; scale-down the same as contain, since the image is larger than the view.

object-fit-size.checks: objectFit none and scale-down show an image smaller than the view at its own size in points (dp), and none crops a larger image to the view even with overflow visible.
object-fit-size.steps: Loads a 40x40 green image with none, the same with scale-down, a bundled 120x120 @3x blue image with none (40 points), and the 600x300 image (red with a blue border) with none and overflow: 'visible'. Passes once all four have loaded; the screenshot checks the sizes.
object-fit-size.shows: Four 48-point views: a green square, another green square, then a blue square, each 40 points and just inside its magenta outline; then a red square (the large image cropped to the view). A square bigger or smaller than its outline (drawn at its size in pixels) or red spilling out of the last view is a failure.

object-fit-blur.checks: objectFit scale-down with blurRadius shows the blurred image at its own size in points (dp), the same size as without the blur.
object-fit-blur.steps: Loads a 120x120 photo into two 144-point views with scale-down, the second with blurRadius 30. Passes once both have loaded (and a moment more, for the blur).
object-fit-blur.shows: Two gray 144-point squares, each with a 120-point photo of a bear on a hillside centered in it: sharp on the left, blurred on the right. A blurred image larger or smaller than the sharp one is a failure.

object-fit-svg.checks: objectFit scale-down and none draw an SVG at its own size in points (dp), as sharp as at that size with contain (Android drew it at its size in pixels and enlarged it, soft and gray).
object-fit-svg.steps: Loads an SVG of 60x60 black and white stripes, one unit wide, with scale-down and none in 72-point views, and with contain in a 60-point view (the reference). Passes once all three have loaded; the screenshot checks the sharpness.
object-fit-svg.shows: Black and white stripes three times: centered in a gray 72-point square, again, then on their own at 60 points, all with the same crisp 1-unit stripes. Soft or gray stripes in the first two are a failure.

object-fit-svg-change.checks: An SVG whose objectFit changes from scale-down to contain while it loads is drawn for contain, sharp at the view's size.
object-fit-svg-change.steps: An 88-point view loads a 60x60 SVG of black and white stripes, one unit wide, from the slow server (8 parts, 150 ms apart) with scale-down, and changes to contain 300 ms later. An 88-point view next to it shows the same SVG with contain from the start. Passes once both have loaded; the screenshot checks the sharpness.
object-fit-svg-change.shows: Black and white stripes filling two squares, both with the same crisp stripes. Soft or gray stripes in the first are a failure.

object-fit-from-cover.checks: Changing objectFit from cover after load, while the image for the new fit loads: on Android the view keeps showing the cover image as it was until then, and iOS shows the new fit at once (Android stretched the cropped image to its own size, squashed with scale-down and enlarged about 12 times with none; changed twice before the first change loaded, it went blank).
object-fit-from-cover.steps: Three 88-point views load a 1600x1000 page of text from the slow server with cache: 'web' (so it isn't on disk) and cover. Once all three have loaded, the first changes to scale-down, the second to none, and the third to scale-down and 150 ms later to none. Passes 800 ms after the change, while the new images are still loading, which is when the screenshot is taken.
object-fit-from-cover.shows: iOS shows the new fit at once: the whole page small with gray above and below, then large letters from the middle of the page twice. Android still shows the cover crop in all three: the middle of the page, small text filling the square. A squashed or enlarged crop, or a blank view, is a failure.

object-fit-style.checks: objectFit in style works, the objectFit prop wins over style, and resizeMode (removed in 10.0), as a prop or in style, is ignored.
object-fit-style.steps: Three 48-point views of the 600x300 image (red with a blue border): style's objectFit: 'contain'; style's contain with the prop objectFit="none"; and resizeMode: 'stretch' in style with resizeMode="contain" as a prop. Passes once all three have loaded; the screenshot checks the fits.
object-fit-style.shows: Contained (half the height, gray above and below), then red only (none, the middle at its own size), then cover (the border only at the top and bottom). A stretched or contained third image is a failure.

object-fit-change.checks: Changing objectFit from contain to none after load shows the middle of the image at its own size, from the full-size image rather than the one decoded for contain.
object-fit-change.steps: Loads a 1600x1000 page of text into two 48-point views: the left with objectFit none from the start, the right with contain, changed to none on its onLoad. Passes 750 ms after the change; the screenshot compares them.
object-fit-change.shows: Large letters from the middle of the page, twice, the same. A blurry or smaller right image is a failure.

description.checks: Changing objectFit after load sends no load events again.

object-fit-events.checks: Changing objectFit after the image has loaded sends no load events again (Android loaded the image again for each fit, with onLoadStart, onLoad and onLoadEnd).
object-fit-events.steps: Loads the 600x300 image (with a run-specific url) with objectFit cover, counting onLoadStart, onLoad and onLoadEnd. After onLoad it changes to contain, cover, then contain again, a second apart. Passes a second after the last change if each event fired once.
object-fit-events.shows: The 600x300 image (red with a blue border) contained in the 48-point view: half the height, gray above and below.

object-fit-events-gif.checks: Changing objectFit after an animated GIF has loaded sends no load events again (Android loaded the image again for each fit, with onLoadStart, onLoad and onLoadEnd).
object-fit-events-gif.steps: Loads a GIF of a jellyfish (with a run-specific url) with objectFit cover, counting onLoadStart, onLoad and onLoadEnd. After onLoad it changes to contain, cover, then contain again, a second apart. Passes a second after the last change if each event fired once.
object-fit-events-gif.shows: The jellyfish contained in the 48-point view, gray above and below; animated, so it isn't compared.

description.checks: Changes after load with objectPosition: a new position sends no load events, and a fade into a positioned image keeps it in place.

position-events.checks: Changing objectPosition after load sends no load events again (Android loaded the image again, with onLoadStart, onLoad and onLoadEnd).
position-events.steps: Loads the 600x300 image (red with a blue border; a run-specific url) with objectFit cover and objectPosition left, counting onLoadStart, onLoad and onLoadEnd. After onLoad it changes to right, then back to left a second later. Passes a second after that if each event fired once.
position-events.shows: The left part of the 600x300 image: its blue border at the left, top and bottom, red to the right edge.

position-events-full-size.checks: Changing objectPosition after load, with downsample={false}, sends no load events again (Android loaded the image again, with onLoadStart, onLoad and onLoadEnd).
position-events-full-size.steps: Loads the 600x300 image (red with a blue border; a run-specific url) with downsample={false}, objectFit cover and objectPosition left, counting onLoadStart, onLoad and onLoadEnd. After onLoad it changes to right, then back to left a second later. Passes a second after that if each event fired once.
position-events-full-size.shows: The left part of the 600x300 image: its blue border at the left, top and bottom, red to the right edge.

position-events-gif.checks: Changing objectPosition after an animated GIF has loaded sends no load events again (Android loaded the image again, with onLoadStart, onLoad and onLoadEnd).
position-events-gif.steps: Loads a GIF of a jellyfish (a run-specific url) with objectFit cover and objectPosition left, counting onLoadStart, onLoad and onLoadEnd. After onLoad it changes to right, then back to left a second later. Passes a second after that if each event fired once.
position-events-gif.shows: The left part of the jellyfish GIF, cropped to the 48-point square; animated, so it isn't compared.

fade-placeholder-positioned.checks: A transition into an image with objectPosition left cross-dissolves from defaultSource with the image in place (iOS moved the image view during the fade, with its clip already moved, so the view's black background showed at its edge).
fade-placeholder-positioned.steps: A 48-point view on black, with a magenta defaultSource and no source; 500 ms later its source becomes a wide cyan image (600x300) from the slow server (about 350 ms), with cover, objectPosition 'left' and a 1 s transition. A video sample records the view's right 4 pixels.
fade-placeholder-positioned.shows: A cyan square. The recording sees magenta, then blue-violet (halfway), then cyan; black must never appear.

description.checks: objectPosition's values, checked by screenshot: with cover, contain, none and scale-down, with the view's style and other props, changed after load, and for defaultSource.

object-position-cover.checks: objectPosition with cover places the cropped image as CSS's object-position does, with keywords, a percentage, and two values (x, then y).
object-position-cover.steps: Loads the 600x300 image into four 48-point views with cover and objectPosition 'left', 'right', '25%' and 'left 10px'. Passes once all four have loaded; the screenshot checks the positions.
object-position-cover.shows: The 600x300 image (red with a blue border) in four 48-point views, each 96x48 after cover: at the left (its left border shows), at the right (its right border), a quarter of the way along (no side border), and at the left 10 points down (a gray gap at the top, the bottom border cut off).

object-position-contain.checks: objectPosition places an image that leaves room in its view: with contain, none and scale-down, keywords, an object ({ bottom: 4 }) and keyword offsets.
object-position-contain.steps: Six 48-point views, each with a magenta outline just outside where its image should be: the 600x300 image with contain at 'top', 'bottom' and { bottom: 4 }; a 16x16 green image with none at 'left top' and 'right 4px bottom 4px', and with scale-down at 'right'. Passes once all six have loaded; the screenshot checks the positions.
object-position-contain.shows: The red and blue image (48x24) in the top half, the bottom half, then 4 points above the bottom; a small green square in the top-left corner, 4 points from the bottom-right corner, then at the right edge, centered. Each image just inside its magenta outline; one outside its outline is a failure.

object-position-style.checks: objectPosition together with the view's style and other props: a rounded border, overflow visible, tintColor, blurRadius and a transition.
object-position-style.steps: Five 48-point views of the 600x300 image: cover at 'left' with borderRadius 14 and a dark 3-point border; none at 'left top' with overflow: 'visible'; contain at 'top' with tintColor #9324c3; contain at 'bottom' with blurRadius 4; cover at 'left' with a 300 ms transition. Passes once all five have loaded (and a moment more).
object-position-style.shows: The image's left part inside a dark rounded border; the image's top-left corner at its own size, cropped to the view (mostly blue, red in the bottom-right corner); a solid purple 48x24 block in the top half; a blurred red and blue image in the bottom half; the image's left part after its fade. The third and fourth sit inside magenta outlines.

object-position-change.checks: Changing objectPosition after load moves the image to the new position (Android cropped it again for cover).
object-position-change.steps: Four 48-point views of the 600x300 image: cover at 'right' (reference), cover changed from 'left' to 'right' when it loads, contain at 'bottom' (reference), and contain changed from 'top' to 'bottom' at the same time. Passes 750 ms after the change.
object-position-change.shows: Two pairs, each image matching the one to its left: the image's right part (its right border showing) twice, then the image in the bottom half twice, gray above. An image still at the left or the top is a failure.

object-position-default-source.checks: defaultSource is placed at objectPosition too, when the source fails.
object-position-default-source.steps: Two 48-point views with objectFit none and a source the image server answers with a 404, and defaultSource an image in the app of four colored quadrants (red, green, blue, yellow; 80x80 points on iOS, 80 pixels on Android), at 'left top' and 'right bottom'. Passes once both have fired onError.
object-position-default-source.shows: On iOS, each view shows a corner of the larger quadrants image: mostly red with green and blue edges (top-left), then mostly yellow with green and blue edges (bottom-right). On Android the whole quadrants image, smaller than the view, sits in the top-left corner, then the bottom-right corner, with gray around it.

description.checks: downsample decodes large images at about the view's size, keeping them sharp, upright and at their own reported size.

downsample-stripes.checks: downsample decodes a large image at about the view's size, and onLoad still reports the image's own size.
downsample-stripes.steps: Loads a 1024x1024 image of 1-pixel black and white stripes into two 48-point views with cover: the left with downsample, the right with downsample={false}. Passes once both onLoad events report 1024x1024.
downsample-stripes.shows: On iOS, an even gray square (the stripes averaged), then the stripes drawn smaller. On Android, a black square (Glide keeps every nth pixel of a PNG), then wide soft gray bands (the stripes, aliased).

downsample-cover.checks: downsample with cover decodes a wide image large enough to cover a tall view, not to fit in it, and shows it a pixel per pixel on whole pixels (on iOS, centered, it was on a half pixel: blurred).
downsample-cover.steps: Loads a 1600x1000 page of text into two 40x96 views with cover: the left with downsample, the right with downsample={false}. Passes once both onLoad events report 1600x1000.
downsample-cover.shows: Two tall crops of the middle of the page, both sharp: the left smooth (the page averaged to the view's size), the right crisper and more jagged (the whole page drawn smaller). Blurry text on the left is a failure.

downsample-orientation.checks: downsample keeps a JPEG's EXIF orientation: an image stored sideways shows upright, as sharp as without downsample.
downsample-orientation.steps: Loads a JPEG stored sideways with EXIF orientation 6 (800x1200 upright) into two 64x96 views with objectFit="contain": the left with downsample, the right with downsample={false}. Passes once both onLoad events report 800x1200.
downsample-orientation.shows: Two upright blue arrows over the word UP, each in a red frame, equally sharp. A sideways arrow is a failure.

downsample-over-limit.checks: An image over 64 megapixels is decoded at 16 megapixels with downsample={false}, and at its own size with objectFit none on iOS; onLoad and preload report its own size.
downsample-over-limit.steps: Loads a 10000x8000 image, white with a 32x64 black block and 1-pixel black and white stripes in its top left corner, into two 96x64 views, each showing that corner at 1 point per pixel: the left with downsample={false}, zoomed 125 times with a transform; the right with objectFit="none" and objectPosition="left top". Once the left one has loaded, preloads its url. Passes once both onLoad events and the preload report 10000x8000.
downsample-over-limit.shows: Two rectangles, each with a black block over its left third. On iOS the rest of the left one is gray (the stripes, decoded smaller, average out), and the right one has stripes 1 point wide, soft-edged (on tvOS dark and light gray). On Android the rest of both is white: it decodes both at 16 megapixels, keeping every other pixel of the PNG (the white stripes).

downsample-over-limit-shared.checks: objectFit none shows an image over 64 megapixels at its own size on iOS when another view of the url decodes it at 16 megapixels at the same time, from the disk cache (the other view's copy showed, at less than half its size).
downsample-over-limit-shared.steps: Preloads the 10000x8000 striped image of downsample-over-limit to the disk cache only (memoryCache: false), then shows it in the same two views, the right one 100 ms after the left. Passes 3 s after both have loaded (on iOS the right one loads again, without events).
downsample-over-limit-shared.shows: Two rectangles, each with a black block over its left third. On iOS the rest of the left one is gray (the stripes, decoded smaller, average out), and the right one has stripes 1 point wide, soft-edged (on tvOS dark and light gray). On Android the rest of both is white: it decodes both at 16 megapixels, keeping every other pixel of the PNG (the white stripes).

downsample-memory.checks: A view that downsamples an image from the disk cache, after a view showed it at full size, doesn't leave its smaller copy where full-size views look (iOS kept it in the memory cache under the full-size image's key).
downsample-memory.steps: Loads a 1600x1000 page of text into an 80x50 view with downsample={false}; 300 ms after it loads, a 32-point view of the same url (downsampled, from the disk cache); 300 ms after that, another 80x50 view with downsample={false}. Passes once the third has loaded; the screenshot checks its sharpness.
downsample-memory.shows: The whole page small, a 32-point crop of it, then the whole page again, as sharp as the first. A blurrier right page is a failure.

downsample-preload.checks: FastImage.preload, after a view downsampled the image from the disk cache, resolves with the image's own size (iOS resolved with the smaller copy's).
downsample-preload.steps: Loads a 1600x1000 page of text into an 80x50 view with downsample={false}; 300 ms after it loads, a 32-point view of the same url (downsampled); 300 ms after that, preloads the url. Passes when the preload resolves ok with 1600x1000.
downsample-preload.shows: The whole page small, then a 32-point crop of it.

description.checks: downsample decoding an image again or sharing its download: larger and growing views, a view without a size, a GIF, a preload in flight, and the order images start in.

downsample-detail.checks: downsample: a larger view of an image already shown smaller decodes it again at its own size, from the disk cache, without downloading it again.
downsample-detail.steps: Loads a 2048x2048 photo (a url of its own) into a 48-point view with downsample; once it loads, a 96-point view of the same url mounts. Once both have loaded, asks the image server how many times the url was requested: passes at once.
downsample-detail.shows: A photo of orange rocks under a cloudy sky, small, then larger and sharp. A blurry larger photo is a failure.

downsample-grow.checks: downsample: a view that grows after its image loaded decodes it again for the new size, without sending the load events again.
downsample-grow.steps: Loads a 1600x1000 page of text into a 48-point view with downsample; 300 ms after onLoad the view grows to 96 points. Passes a second later if onLoadStart and onLoad fired once each.
downsample-grow.shows: A 96-point crop of the middle of the page, the text sharp. Blurry text (the small decode enlarged) is a failure.

downsample-no-size.checks: downsample: an image in a view with no size until it loads (sized from onLoad) still loads.
downsample-no-size.steps: Loads a 600x300 photo with downsample and no style, inside a 48-point gray square; onLoad sizes it 48 wide and 24 tall. Passes once it has been laid out with a width.
downsample-no-size.shows: A photo of green hills across the top half of the gray square, gray below. An empty gray square is a failure.

downsample-gif.checks: downsample: an animated GIF loads and plays, and onLoad reports its own size.
downsample-gif.steps: Loads a 500x281 GIF of a jellyfish into a 32-point view with downsample. Passes when onLoad reports 500x281.
downsample-gif.shows: The jellyfish cropped to the small square; animated, so it isn't compared.

downsample-preloading.checks: downsample: a view of an image that's still being preloaded shares the preload's download, decodes it to cover the view (cropped, not stretched), and onLoad reports its full size (iOS downloaded it again).
downsample-preloading.steps: Preloads a 1600x1000 page of text from the slow server (about a second); once the server has the request, a 40x96 view with downsample loads the same source. Passes when onLoad reports 1600x1000 and the server got one request.
downsample-preloading.shows: A tall crop of the middle of the page, the text at its usual shape. Squashed text (the page stretched to the tall view) is a failure.

downsample-order.checks: downsample: images mounted together start loading in the order of their views, left to right (iOS started them as UIKit laid the views out, last first).
downsample-order.steps: Mounts six 32-point cells, each with an image filling it, of a 2048x2048 photo at six new urls, with downsample. Passes once all six have started and loaded, and, on iOS with the New Architecture, their onLoadStart events came left to right (Android loads in another order, so the order is only checked on iOS).
downsample-order.shows: Six small copies of a photo of orange rocks under a cloudy sky, in a row.

description.checks: downsample={false} keeps an image that's zoomed in on with a transform sharp.

downsample-zoom.checks: downsample={false} decodes an image at full size, so a view zoomed in on with a transform (as a pinch-to-zoom viewer does) stays sharp (Android decoded it at about the view's size either way).
downsample-zoom.steps: Loads a 1600x1000 page of text into two 80x50 views drawn 4 times larger with a transform, each clipped to a 140x88 area showing its top-left corner: the left with downsample (the default), the right with downsample={false}. Passes once both have loaded (and a moment more).
downsample-zoom.shows: The first lines of the page, enlarged, twice: blurry on the left, sharp on the right. Blurry text on the right is a failure.

description.checks: An image in a view far larger than the screen shows: a still image, one cross-dissolving to a new source, a GIF and a placeholder url.

large-view.checks: An image in a view far larger than the screen shows (on Android its bitmap was the view's size, about 160 MB, and the app crashed drawing it).
large-view.steps: Loads a 20x20 image of four colored squares into a 2400x2400 view with cover, drawn 20 times smaller with a transform. Passes once it has loaded (and a moment more).
large-view.shows: A 120x120 square of four colors: red, green, blue and yellow quadrants. The app closing is a failure.

large-view-fade.checks: transition's betweenImages in a view far larger than the screen (on Android the fade copied what the view showed into a bitmap the view's size, about 160 MB, and the app crashed drawing it).
large-view-fade.steps: The large-view case, with transition { duration: 300, betweenImages: true }: once the image loads, its source changes to the same image at another url, which cross-dissolves from it. Passes once both have loaded (and a moment more).
large-view-fade.shows: A 120x120 square of four colors: red, green, blue and yellow quadrants. The app closing is a failure.

large-view-gif.checks: A GIF in a view far larger than the screen shows (on Android each frame was cropped to the view's size, about 160 MB, and the app crashed drawing it).
large-view-gif.steps: Loads an 80x80 GIF that plays once, magenta then cyan, into a 2400x2400 view with cover, drawn 20 times smaller with a transform. Passes once it has loaded (and a moment more).
large-view-gif.shows: A 120x120 cyan square. The app closing is a failure.

large-view-placeholder.checks: A placeholder url in a view far larger than the screen shows while the image loads (on Android it was loaded at the view's size, about 160 MB, and the app crashed drawing it).
large-view-placeholder.steps: The large-view case, with the image from the slow server (about 4 s) and a placeholder url of the logo, which shows meanwhile. Passes once the image has loaded (and a moment more).
large-view-placeholder.shows: A 120x120 square of four colors: red, green, blue and yellow quadrants. The app closing is a failure.

description.checks: downsample={false} decodes at full size an image that's on disk but not in memory while a downsampled view of it loads.

downsample-from-disk.checks: downsample={false} decodes at full size an image that's on disk but not in memory (as after the app restarts) when a downsampled view of it mounts at the same time (the downsampled view's copy showed, blurry).
downsample-from-disk.steps: Preloads a 1600x1000 page of text to the disk cache only (memoryCache: false), then mounts two 80x50 views of it together, drawn 4 times larger with a transform and clipped to 140x88: the left with downsample, the right with downsample={false}. Passes once both have loaded (and a moment more).
downsample-from-disk.shows: The first lines of the page, enlarged, twice: blurry on the left, sharp on the right. Blurry text on the right is a failure.

description.checks: Loading: props that don't reload, source changes, onLoadStart and onProgress, cache: 'web' and cookies.

no-reload.checks: Changing a prop that doesn't affect loading doesn't load the image again (Android reloaded it on every prop update).
no-reload.steps: Loads a 600x300 photo; once it has loaded, changes accessibilityLabel every 200 ms for a second. Passes if onLoadStart didn't fire again.
no-reload.shows: A photo of green hills, cropped to the square.

source-swap.checks: Changing source over and over keeps loading each new image (#384: Android kept the view in its progress list under every url it had loaded, which kept the view and its Activity alive).
source-swap.steps: Loads three 120x120 photos in turn in one view, moving to the next on each onLoad, four times, so it ends on the second. Passes when the last one loads.
source-swap.shows: A black and white photo of a misty forest.

load-start-once.checks: onLoadStart fires once per load (iOS sent it twice when source and onLoadStart were set in the same update).
load-start-once.steps: Loads a 200x200 photo with onLoadStart and onLoad set from the first render. Passes once onLoad has fired, if onLoadStart fired once.
load-start-once.shows: A photo of a pug wrapped in a blanket.

progress.checks: onProgress events have a progress (loaded / total, 0 to 1), and the last one is 1.
progress.steps: Loads a 2048x2048 photo (a new url each run) that the server sends with a Content-Length. Each onProgress must have a total above 0, loaded between 0 and the total and never going down, and progress equal to loaded / total; passes at onLoad if there was at least one and the last had everything loaded and progress 1.
progress.shows: A photo of a fjord seen from a cliff.

progress-unknown-size.checks: onProgress for an image whose size is unknown (no Content-Length): none sent, or each with a real total (Android sent a total of -1 and iOS -1 or 0, so loaded / total was negative or infinite).
progress-unknown-size.steps: Loads the 2048x2048 photo from the image server's chunked/ path, which sends it without a Content-Length. Passes at onLoad if there were no onProgress events, or each had a total above 0, loaded between 0 and the total, and the last one 1.
progress-unknown-size.shows: A photo of a fjord seen from a cliff.

progress-gzip.checks: onProgress for an image sent gzip-compressed, whose Content-Length is smaller than the image the client ends up with: loaded never goes past the total.
progress-gzip.steps: Loads the 2048x2048 photo from the image server's gzip/ path. Passes at onLoad if each onProgress had loaded between 0 and the total and the last one was 1 (or there were none).
progress-gzip.shows: A photo of a fjord seen from a cliff.

web-cache.checks: cache: 'web' follows the server's caching headers (#280: Android sent every request to the network).
web-cache.steps: Loads a 200x200 photo with cache: 'web' from the image server's max-age/ path (cacheable for an hour), then mounts a new view that loads it again, then replaces it with an empty view. Passes if the server got one request for it.
web-cache.shows: An empty gray square: the image view is gone by the end.

web-cache-avif.checks: cache: 'web' keeps an AVIF in the HTTP cache (iOS requested it again: SDWebImage's format check doesn't know AVIF).
web-cache-avif.steps: Loads an AVIF of four colored quadrants with cache: 'web' from the image server's max-age/ path (cacheable for an hour), then mounts a new view that loads it again, then replaces it with an empty view. Passes if the server got one request for it.
web-cache-avif.shows: An empty gray square: the image view is gone by the end.

cookies.checks: Image requests send the app's cookies, and keep the ones they get (Android sent no cookies with images: React Native's shared OkHttp client has an empty cookie jar).
cookies.steps: Gets two cookies with fetch (this run's values), then loads the React logo from the image server's cookie/ path, which answers 403 without both and sets a cookie of its own. On onLoad, asks the server which cookies a fetch sends: passes if the image's cookie is among them.
cookies.shows: The React logo (light blue) on the gray square. An empty gray square means the image was refused (no cookies sent).

description.checks: onProgress for a data: image.

progress-data-uri.checks: onProgress for a data: image: iOS sends one event, which has a progress (loaded / total, 1); Android sends none.
progress-data-uri.steps: Loads an 8x8 yellow PNG from a data: uri. Passes at onLoad if each onProgress (if any) had a total above 0, loaded up to the total and progress equal to loaded / total, and the last one 1.

description.checks: onProgress for many images on one url while others on it mount and unmount.

progress-shared-url.checks: onProgress for many images on one url while others on it mount and unmount: every image loads, with onProgress only after its onLoadStart and before its onLoad (Android went through the url's list of views on the download thread while the UI thread changed it, which threw and failed the download for every image; and a view that mounted while progress was waiting to be sent could get it before its own onLoadStart).
progress-shared-url.steps: Forty 6-point images with onProgress load one url from the slow server while ten more on that url mount and unmount every other frame, for eight rounds, a new url each round; a round ends once the forty have loaded. Passes after the eight rounds if there was no onError, each of the forty got onProgress before onLoad, never going back, ending at 1 and none after, and no mounted image got onProgress before its onLoadStart.
progress-shared-url.shows: Nothing: the images are removed once it has passed, leaving an empty area.

description.checks: onProgress reaching the right images when downloads are shared, urls are written differently or the server holds part of the download.

progress-after-load.checks: An image gets no onProgress after its onLoad when another image downloads the same url (Android sent a url's progress to every image that had loaded it, until it loaded another source).
progress-after-load.steps: Loads a 200x200 photo from the slow server with cache: 'web' (the slow server sends no cache headers, so it isn't cached) and onProgress; once it loads, a second image downloads the same url. Passes once the second has loaded, if it got onProgress and the first got none after its onLoad.
progress-after-load.shows: Two photos of a pug wrapped in a blanket, side by side.

progress-url-form.checks: onProgress for a url with its scheme in capitals (HTTP://) (Android looked images up by their url as written, while downloads reported it as OkHttp writes it, lowercase, so these urls got no onProgress).
progress-url-form.steps: Loads a 200x200 photo from the slow server at a url starting with HTTP://. Passes at onLoad if there was at least one onProgress, each with a total above 0, loaded never going down and progress equal to loaded / total, and the last one 1.
progress-url-form.shows: A photo of a pug wrapped in a blanket.

progress-cache-key.checks: onProgress for two images of different sizes and urls with the same cacheKey, loading at the same time (Android looked images up by their own url, so the image whose url wasn't downloaded got no onProgress, and it downloaded each size).
progress-cache-key.steps: A 32-point and a 64-point image load the same 200x200 photo from the slow server at two urls (another query) with one cacheKey. Passes once both have loaded, if each got onProgress before its onLoad, never going back, ending at 1 and none after, and the server got one request on Android (which shares downloads by cache key) or two on iOS (SDWebImage shares them by url).
progress-cache-key.shows: Two photos of a pug wrapped in a blanket, small then larger, side by side.

progress-held-bytes.checks: onProgress comes for the bytes that have arrived while the rest of the download is held up (Android sent the progress for bytes only once the next ones arrived, so the first part's progress waited for the rest).
progress-held-bytes.steps: Loads a 200x200 photo from the slow server, which sends the first of its 8 parts and holds the rest until the case releases it: on the first onProgress, or after 3 s. Passes once the image loads, if onProgress came before the release.
progress-held-bytes.shows: A photo of a pug wrapped in a blanket.

description.checks: Android's downloads waiting to start: the priority and url a waiting download has as requests for it join and leave (three checks on one set of images).

priority-lowered.checks: A waiting download's priority after a more urgent request for it leaves, and the url it downloads. Android only: iOS's downloads are SDWebImage's, whose order depends on timing.
priority-lowered.steps: Nothing to load on iOS: passes if the app is still running a moment after it mounts.

description.checks: An image with priority: 'high' that starts loading after twenty others is downloaded before most of them.

download-priority.checks: A priority: 'high' image that starts loading after twenty others is downloaded before most of them (Android handed 16 downloads to OkHttp at once, which sends them in the order they came, so the high one was 17th).
download-priority.steps: Twenty images from the slow server, each its own url, load with normal priority, and the server holds their responses. Once it has their first request, one more image loads with priority: 'high', and half a second later the server sends the responses. Passes when all have loaded and at most 12 of the twenty were requested before the high one (those the platform sends at once, 5 or 6, and some started with it).
download-priority.shows: Twenty-one tiny tiles of the same photo (a bear on rocks, under a pale sky): two rows of ten, then one. A blank spot is an image that failed.

description.checks: Downloads shared by several images of one url (one request for all of them), through unmounts, errors and responses without a Content-Length, and a download that stalls.
description.steps: The images come from the slow server, which sends each in eight parts with a pause between them, and can hold the rest of a response until the case releases it. The images have no background, so where nothing shows the screen is white.

shared-download-sizes.checks: Two images of one url at different sizes, loading at the same time, share one download, and each gets onProgress up to 1 (Glide only shares a download between requests for the same size, so Android downloaded it twice).
shared-download-sizes.steps: Loads the photo from the slow server in a 32-point and a 64-point image at once. Passes when both have loaded, the last onProgress each got before its onLoad was 1, and the server got one request.
shared-download-sizes.shows: A small (32-point) and a large (64-point) photo of a pug in a blanket, side by side.

shared-download-cancel.checks: A download shared by two images goes on for one of them when the other unmounts.
shared-download-cancel.steps: Loads one url from the slow server in a small and a large image; the server holds it halfway. Once both have had onProgress, the small one unmounts and the server sends the rest. Passes when the large one has loaded and the server got one request.
shared-download-cancel.shows: Blank space where the small image was, then the large (64-point) photo of a pug in a blanket.

shared-download-error.checks: Two images of one url that 404s, at different sizes and loading at the same time, both get onError with the status in their error.
shared-download-error.steps: Loads a missing image from the slow server in a small and a large image at once. Passes when both have had onError and both errors mention 404 (onLoad fails it).
shared-download-error.shows: Blank space: the two images (32 and 64 points) have no background and nothing loads.

shared-download-chunked.checks: Two images of one url at different sizes share one download when its response has no Content-Length (Android didn't share a response of unknown length: the second image downloaded it again once the first's had arrived).
shared-download-chunked.steps: Loads the photo from the slow server, sent without a Content-Length, in a 32-point and a 64-point image at once. Passes when both have loaded and the server got one request.
shared-download-chunked.shows: A small (32-point) and a large (64-point) photo of a pug in a blanket, side by side.

chunked-download-cancel.checks: An image unmounts while it downloads a response without a Content-Length, and a later image of that url still loads (on Android, closing the response on the main thread would read the socket and throw NetworkOnMainThreadException, so the call is cancelled instead).
chunked-download-cancel.steps: Loads the photo from the slow server, sent without a Content-Length, in a small image; the server holds it halfway. The image unmounts, half a second later the server is released, and a large image of the same url mounts. Passes when the large one loads, with no onError.
chunked-download-cancel.shows: Blank space where the small image was, then the large (64-point) photo of a pug in a blanket.

stalled-download.checks: A download that gets nothing for 15 seconds fails with onError (Android's client had no timeouts, so the image, and every request sharing its download, waited forever).
